utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. At the end of the day you asked me regarding exhibits that were referred to in the Milosevic transcript of this witness's testimony. I have gone through and checked, Your Honour. There are a number that I would like to bring to your attention and give you the cross-reference numbers, because in Milosevic it had a different number, obviously, than we have in our case. At page 40 -- at page 2042 of the transcript, there is a reference to Milosevic Exhibit 62, which is the hand-drawn map of the witness's municipality, that is our Exhibit P43. At page 2089 of the transcript, there is a reference to the log-book which was Exhibit 63 in Milosevic and which is our 1331. At page 2096, there is a reference to the two statements, the ICTY statements, of the witness which were given the Exhibit Number 64 and 65 in Milosevic, which we have given Exhibit Numbers P2298 and P2299, with 2298 being his statement from 25 April 1999, and 2299 being his 31 August 2001 statement. Also shown to the witness was Exhibit 17 from the Milosevic case at page 2059 of the transcript. That is our Exhibit P1325 already in evidence. And Exhibit 18 in the Milosevic case at page 2058 of the transcript, photographs of uniforms, which is our Exhibit 1326, already in evidence. And finally, at page 2071, there was reference to Milosevic Exhibit 3, map 11, which is our Exhibit P25, showing the deportation route from Urosevac, Ferizaj. And to the extent that those are not already in evidence, I would tender them at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How does -- or how do the statements feature in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was extensive cross-examination by Mr. Milosevic about the statements, and I think Mr. Tapuskovic of the amici also did cross-examination. At page 2096 Judge May indicated that: "We need the statements. Can we have copies, please, there's going to be cross-examination about it." And then there was extensive cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bucaliu.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your evidence will now continue. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration which you took at the beginning of the evidence yesterday will continue to supply to your evidence today. The next counsel to ask questions of you will be Mr. Cepic. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. However, before I start my cross-examination, by your leave I would like to address you with a few words only and it has to do with the exhibits that my learned friend Mr. Hannis just referred to now. Actually, I seem to be one of the people who are not very technically minded and have a lot of trouble with this new system. I spent all day yesterday looking for these statements that my learned friend mentioned just now. Last night in accordance with 92 bis only the transcript was referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the references, the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give me again the numbers of the statements -- that's the -- I take it you're referring to 2298 and 2299?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes, exactly, Your Honour, because yesterday in a package I just found the transcripts from the Milosevic case, and I tried to find -- to find in the system those statements, but probably I haven't got enough experience with these electronic devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, it's my understanding from my case manager that 2298 and 2299 are the next two numbers on the list but they are not in the system yet. They have been disclosed to the Defence, but they are not in the electronic court system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, this is very unfortunate because we -- when we addressed this issue before of what the extent of a 92 bis (D) statement was, Ms. Carter ensured me that it included all of the exhibits, and that's why witnesses statements who were also presented in part in the course of the examination-in-chief were entirely regarded as 92 bis (D) witnesses. So if you're going to be relying on the exhibits, then they should have been intimated as part of the package, shouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I can explain the difference in this situation. In this situation, as opposed to most of the other Milosevic 92 bis witnesses, his statement was not tendered as a 92 bis (B), he was led as a live witness. During cross-examination when Mr. Milosevic started doing extensive cross-examination on the statements, that's when the Court indicated a need for the statements. And now, since we've offered the transcript with references to those materials, I thought it would be helpful to tender to the Court the statements that are referred to in the cross-examination. In most of the other cases, the witness was presented as a 92 bis, the statement was tendered in the Prosecution's direct examination. A short summary was read and then the witness was turned over for cross-examine. In this witness's case, he was led as a live witness and then during cross-examination his statements were gone into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Cepic, the material was disclosed. You should be capable of finding it. I accept that there's a measure of confusion here, but please continue with your cross-examination. If later you discover that there is something crucial that you've been somehow or other made prevented from dealing with, you'll need to make an appropriate application for us to address. But let's proceed with the examination today.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bajram. I'm Djuro Cepic, one of the Defence lawyers for Vladimir Lazarevic. Before I move on, before I start putting questions to you, can you please tell me how I should pronounce your last name. Is it Bucaliu or Bukaliu?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: My last name is Bucaliu.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bucaliu. In your statement you described that on the 25th of March you came to the railway station in Urosevac, where you worked, and that your supervisor told you that as of that day you were no longer employed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the morning of the 24th -- in fact, 25th of May I went to work, as usual. And when I arrived there I asked about my other Albanian colleagues, and my boss told me that as of today we have taken orders for you not to work. You must show up here, but you are not supposed to work. I asked him: Why is this? What has happened? He said: We've taken orders from above. That was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just to be sure about the date, it was the 25th of March, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Of March.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean the night after the strikes started, 25th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bucaliu. I will try to put very specific questions to you so that we would deal with them as fast as possible, so could you please just give me shorter answers. Thank you in advance. You also say that you were in your village on the 2nd of April when the army came with four or five tanks, you said. In your statement that the Prosecutor just referred to as P2298 dated the 24th and 25th of April, 1999, you read that statement and signed it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And you clearly understood everything that you stated in it, right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You say that soldiers came who wore green berets, that is on page 2, paragraph 3, and you say that they had metal badges saying "VJ" on them, right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And what would you say to me if I were to say to you that the army of Yugoslavia never had such insignia?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: You may think so, but what I have already said, it's true, even though seven years have passed and I may not guarantee that they were metal insignia. But if I have stated it in my statement that it -- that they were metal insignia, then it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that your best recollection, in view of all of these events, was when you made this particular statement, the one that I am quoting now, that is to say, in the immediate aftermath. Your recollection must have been much better then than now, seven years later, right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next sentence you describe tanks, and you say that their barrels were not extended. Do you know that not a single tank in the world can pull its barrels in and out?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am fully aware of that and I know that because I have already mentioned that I did my military service. Maybe there are some translation mistakes. I never said that the barrel could be pulled in and out, but maybe it's a mistake, a translation mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, a few moments ago I asked you whether you had read out, understood, and signed the statement that you gave in 1999, the one that I am referring to now, and your answer was affirmative. How come now that you do not understand and that there are mistakes in the said statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have hard copies of the Albanian version of this witness's statement, which it may be helpful if he has in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Cepic, we should have the statement on the screen. That's P2298.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, I agree, Your Honour. As far as we understood the Prosecutor this morning, it is in the system. [In English] If I correctly understood my learned friend it is in the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's my understanding the statements are not in the system yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I would kindly ask that they be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would it help if we put the English on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you allow me, I've got enough hard copies in my possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's sufficient if the English is put on the ELMO and the witness has the Albanian copy. Can you direct us to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I asked witness about -- that is on the second page, paragraph 3, line 4: "The military tanks were dark green in colour with chains as wheels and no extended long barrel."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have the passage, Mr. Bucaliu?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not yet. Can I please have a copy in Albanian -- oh, can I see it on the screen in Albanian if that is possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you not got an Albanian copy in your hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I need some time to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Go to the third paragraph which starts: -- Yes, second paragraph: "Staro Selo was first occupied on 2/4/99."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you'll see the reference to military tanks being dark green in colour. Now, read that sentence to us, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The military tanks were of dark green olive colour with chains instead of the wheels and without any long barrel." I mean small cannon here because, as you know, there are different calibre cannons and what I meant was a small-calibre cannon, not the barrel that can be pulled in and out. The meaning was that it was a small cannon, a small-calibre cannon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, are you a ballistics expert?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not, and I never thought I was one. But I am familiar with armaments because, as I said, I did my military service in the former Yugoslav army and I am more or less familiar with its arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But you were not in tank units, right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not; that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on you say - and we heard that yesterday - that you talked to a major, as he had introduced himself, and he told you to stay. However, in this statement from 1999 you say that you actually talked to a soldier. Now, what is correct? Did you talk to a soldier or a major?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The correct version is that I talked with a major, a military major.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, these houses where the army was located at the entrance into the village, how far away are they from your house?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: These houses are some 500 metres away from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And you cannot see them since they're all single-storeyed houses, right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see these houses very well from my house because they were not one storey; they were two- and three-storey houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Aren't all houses in the village either single-storeyed or just two-storeyed? You don't live in a city, right, you live in a village?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I live in a village, that's true, but the houses in our village are up to five-storey houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that your own house has five storeys?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that I lived in a five-storey house. Mine was a two-storey house. It was burned and it is still not repaired.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So in the village there are some five-storeyed houses too. Your house is a two-storey house, and the houses at the entrance into the village are single-storeyed or two-storeys. So how can you see the entrance into the village when in between you have five-storeyed houses, inter alia?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between my house and the houses where the army was positioned, there wasn't any house in between. It consists only of meadows and fields, so nothing prevented my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on you say --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or actually, can we look at the map for a moment? It is P43. Could we please have this map on e-court, P43, Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, on this map can we see your house? Has it been marked on the upper right-hand corner? There is a cross-roads and there is this dark spot; is that your house?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not my house. My house is on this side here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I would just like to have something clarified to me. And why is this other house marked with a dark spot, on the other side?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But the entrance into the village is from the road Urosevac-Gnjilane, so it's not by your house - isn't that right? - as we can see on this map?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: My house is in the internal part of the village, some 600 metres away from the Gjilan road.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 that we quoted a few moments ago you say that the army took up positions at the beginning of the road, that is to say at the entrance into the village. Could you please show us on the map where this actually is, where you actually turn off the Gnjilane-Urosevac road.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entrance is here, and the houses was situated here in those houses on both sides of the street, here and street, at the entrance to the street --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, you need to make a mark on the map with that pen before we can see what you're doing. So can you make these marks, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly. Here and here. These were the houses which the army took over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the question, though, was where you actually turn off the Gnjilane-Urosevac or Ferizaj road.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the road Gjilan-Ferizaj. The turn is here, the one I marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see on this drawing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just for the avoidance of doubt, you've marked houses on either side of the road near the junction with the road from Gnjilane to Ferizaj. All right. Carry on, please, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bucaliu, in your statement you said that they were stationed in three houses respectively on both sides, not in all of those places as you marked just now on this map. As far as I can see on the map, several houses are marked. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's impossible with the equipment to do the sort of detailed marking you're talking about. This is, I have to say, not an appropriate line to follow in cross-examination when the equipment that we're using couldn't possibly --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- enable the witness to be any more accurate than he has been. Let's get on with it to material issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to this map, we can conclude that there were some houses between your house and the houses where the soldiers were billeted. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all correct. I already told you, and you can see it clearly on the map, where my house is and where they were stationed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bucaliu. We are now to move on, since unfortunately the map isn't sufficiently clear for us to explore it any further--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, who actually drew the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I, Your Honour, I drew this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Were soldiers billeted in the house of Maksim Perovic?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army -- rather, the soldiers were not stationed in the house of Maksim Perovic, but moved around and visited the houses of the Serbs, of our Serb neighbours. As I said earlier, they were stationed at the beginning.. at the entrance to the village there, but they moved around and went around to the houses of the Serbs in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. Thank you. Mr. Bucaliu, how do you explain the contradiction. In your statement of 1999 you said that the army took up Albanian houses. I will quote: "The army was stationed in six houses that belonged to Albanians." This is page 2, paragraph 3. And today you are stating that they were billeted in the Serbian houses, Mr. Bucaliu

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that then or today. They were not stationed in Serb houses. I will repeat again that the army was stationed in Albanian houses at the entrance into the village. They would go every now and then to Serbian houses as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. [In English] "... different houses of our Serb neighbours." [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bucaliu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me go back, Mr. Bucaliu, to a question earlier. You were asked a question: The army -- rather, the soldiers were not stationed inside the house of Maksim Perovic -- sorry. The question you were asked was: Were soldiers billeted in the house -- houses of Maksim Perovic? And your answer started: "The army -- rather, the soldiers were not stationed inside the house of Maksim Perovic." You then said something about houses at the entrance into the village. Could you tell us again what you said about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The houses at the entrance into the village are all Albanian houses, and that's where the Serbian soldiers were stationed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the transcript says: "They moved in different houses of our Serbian neighbours, houses that were at the entrance into the village." Did you actually say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. It could be a mistake, because the houses at the entrance into the village are Albanian houses. Inside the village there are Serbian houses where the Serbian soldiers would stay every now and then. They would go there to have coffee or to chat with the Serbian neighbours, but they were stationed in the houses which are at the entrance into the village and which are Albanian houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, I'll have that checked and we'll advise you as soon as possible whether there was a mistake in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, please. I would be so grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bucaliu, we now come to the 4th of April. Yesterday you stated that on that day a truck owned by you was taken away from a front yard of one of your Serb neighbours. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, because they had taken the truck that we had left in the yard of a Serbian neighbour. That truck belonged to my uncle.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Why did you state yesterday as well as in the Milosevic case that you were the owner of the truck?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that I was the owner. My uncle left the truck with me, so for that time you can call it as my own property. So I took this truck to my Serbian neighbour for it to be safer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of March, 2002, you testified in the Milosevic case. At page 2062, beginning from line 10, you mentioned the following: "Then they took away my truck." Yesterday, this is in the transcript page 71, line 5, you state that they truck away your truck.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm saying that this truck belonged to my uncle. So from the moment my uncle brought the truck to my place, I regarded it as my own truck. So that's why I moved it to my neighbour's yard, for it to be safer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You will agree that the issue of ownership is one of the principal issues. How come you provide us with different answers in just two different days?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer that question for the moment, Mr. Bucaliu, we wish to confer on the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, we are all agreed that none of your cross-examination is assisting us in any way, and unless you can proceed to something productive then we're going to bring it to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I understood, Your Honour. I do apologise to this Honourable Trial Chamber. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, please try to proceed to something that may assist us in determining the very important issues that are before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bucaliu, I believe you are familiar with the fact that at that time it was the state of war. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In the territory of the entire Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Isn't that also correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the entire territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, but in our area that was the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in such situations regulation is put in place, according to which citizens need to surrender their vehicles for the use of the army should it become necessary and that they are -- they enjoy the right to be compensated for it?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, since sir asked me, I will elaborate it now. The truck was in my Serb neighbour's yard. The Serb soldiers went to him and asked him: Whose is this truck? Please, you asked me the questions -- question, let me answer it now. So my Serb neighbour answered: It belongs to my neighbour. The Serbian neighbour came to me, took the keys of the truck, and he was kind of scared of these soldiers. He said to me: Please give me the keys as soon as possible because they might even do something to the truck. So he went back with the keys and they wanted to see what is inside the truck. They didn't even allow me to take the documents from the truck. They said to me: What do you -- what kind of documents do you want? They just started the truck and left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bucaliu, the question you were asked was whether you were aware that there were regulations in times of war authorising the military to take control of vehicles. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am aware of that. And I know from the rules of war that in such cases vehicles can be seized for the needs of the army, but in those cases they should provide you with a document that states that this truck was taken from this and that person. So that's why I'm saying in this case it wasn't the case that the lawyer is speaking of. It was looting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: After the war did you ask for your property to be returned, did you ask for it in writing?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: My uncle, through this neighbour of mine in whose yard the truck was, he asked for his truck to be returned to him. He actually even authorised the neighbour, he put the truck on his name so he was hoping that that could be a way for him to get his truck back. But the answers that the neighbour got was that the truck was somewhere with the army but could not be returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether you personally or your uncle submitted an application to the army for the property to be returned.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, and my uncle himself, we did not ask for our truck from the army. I said that it was my neighbour who did that. We were doing this through the neighbour and the neighbour was refused many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I presume you don't have any documents according -- that would prove that?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents are in Ferizaj, if that is important. I can bring them to you. I don't have them with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on you state that on the 5th of April the army left your village. On the same day, in the afternoon, some members of a paramilitary formation came and you identified them as being part of the Serbian Chetnik Movement. They restricted your movement, they wouldn't allow you to leave the village, and they introduced a curfew between 7.00 p.m. and 7.00 a.m. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You remained in the village until the 14th in the morning, when you are advised by your imam on the murder and then the entire village, some 5 to 600 people, leave the village of their own will and move towards Urosevac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just one correction for transcript, please. Line 18 I said 500 to 600 people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Actually, that's how I would read the transcript as it stands, but I agree normally it would say 500 to 600.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But 5 to 600 people is the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you explain me this: Since such measures were introduced such as you have described, how did you manage to leave the village, these 5 to 600 people?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain it to you and I've already done that in my statement. But I will describe it to you shortly. So after we received this news about our neighbours being killed, people in the village were terrified. It is true that on this day we were aware of the fact that we were encircled and that we were told not to leave the village, but instinctively on that day people just wanted to save themselves and decided to flee. The part where we -- from where we escaped, it's a flat part, it's kind of a valley, it is possible for them not to have seen us. I'm not sure when I say this, but this is how we escaped.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. In the evening you arrive in Urosevac and you joined your family. On the 15th, in the morning, you arrived at the train station, you boarded the train, as mentioned in the log-book you brought here, and the train number was 7893. To make it easier for you, this is page K0218517 of the transportation log-book, and you brought that document to be used in the Milosevic case. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The same train bearing the number 7892 was used by you to return to Urosevac, and those were the only two trains on that day which went through that train station. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The next day you boarded the train with the same number and you leave for Macedonia. And as it is stated in the log-book, there were only two trains that day. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gerxhaliu -- I apologise. Mr. Bucaliu, I truly apologise for confusing you with someone else. How can we distinguish between a freight and a passenger train by reading this log-book?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The passenger trains differ from the freight trains in this log-book according to the digit numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you explain us what the distinction is in terms of numbers?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The passenger trains, as I said yesterday, are marked by three- and four-digit numbers, while the freight trains are marked by five-digit numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bucaliu. There is no signature in this log-book since you were not the person keeping it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you ever keep a train log-book?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. From 1981 to 1987 and now from 2002 to present.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we should clarify something. You say that you have been keeping such log-books from 2002 until the present. But from what I understood from the transcript and according to what you stated yesterday, you were a gas station operator and there was no mention of you keeping a log-book.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did work at a gas station, but now I work in a railway station and I do keep log-book since 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, yesterday in answer to one of the questions by the OTP you stated that you work at the gas station in your village, and yet today we hear something you haven't stated so far?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we have a reference to that transcript from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we'll need some time to clarify this and we shouldn't waste any more time to the Chamber. Perhaps we can clarify and verify this and then we will let you know at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, are you challenging this log-book?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So are you saying it's falsified or -- I mean, what are you saying about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, but I would like just to check is it -- was it -- the witness able to -- to give us information about this diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're not challenging it at the moment? You're just exploring -- you're sort of fishing for possible loop-holes, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I just would like to know: Was the witness qualified to -- to give us information about this diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that up until 1987 you kept log-books. I presume that was up until the moment when you caused a train accident in which several people sustained serious injuries and you were suspended for six months. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer that question. I'd like to know the relevance of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: From --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: From 1987 until 1999 this witness wasn't in charge to fill this diary, to have any contact with diary, to know anything about diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Because he was a cashier in the cargo department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but what's the relevance of the question? If you're accepting that he -- he kept a diary up until 1987, what's the issue that the question you've just asked goes to?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did he knows the rules? For example, if they change something in the meantime, numbers, codes, rules of transport company, railway transport company of Belgrade. He wasn't in charge for that. He was in charge for -- as a cashier in cargo department, not for diaries, not for transport diaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are you saying, Mr. Cepic, that he has misrepresented the diary yesterday -- the log-book yesterday? Are you saying that he has --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- given false information? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I've been trying to find, is he qualified to give us correct information? I've been trying. I'm not from transport company; I haven't got that experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we will not prevent you from pursuing the line that you're pursuing, but we will not allow you to ask the question that was posed. Now, Mr. Hannis, do you have something else to say on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Related to that, Your Honour, if he was going to ask a question like that, I have no documents released to me. I would like to know the foundation for that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the question is irrelevant --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- to the issue here, although the line of examination may not be irrelevant. So you'll need to proceed along proper lines, Mr. Cepic, in exploring this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I do apologise for the lack of my experience in the cross-examination. I've been trying to do my best before this Honourable Trial Chamber. I think that my colleagues will challenge this topic, so I will move on, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, they may encounter the same difficulty as you, Mr. Cepic, but we shall see.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bucaliu, you mentioned that you gave assistance to the so-called KLA by transporting a soldier. Could you tell me when this happened and how did it come about?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say I assisted the KLA. I said that I helped the son of a friend of mine, to transport him from one place to another. That person was a member in the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But just now you confirmed that that person was a member of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was a member of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You were also -- you were also asked, Mr. Bucaliu, when this happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This happened in 1998. It must have been October of 1998. I am not very sure about the exact time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In the transcript in the Milosevic case on page 2123, line 5 -- or rather, lines 5 through 8, you said that at that time there was fighting in Sar Planina between the KLA on the one side, and that in that fighting that particular soldier of the KLA was wounded. Could you tell me in what village you actually took in this wounded soldier of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took him from Varrosh village and took him to Softaj village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: All of that is in the municipality of Urosevac, these two villages that you just referred to, right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Both villages are part of Ferizaj municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Were there any other contacts in that period, that is to say in 1998, with the KLA? On your part, that is.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any contacts with the KLA during that period. And until the end of the war, I never had any contacts with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And are you aware of terrorist attacks launched by the so-called KLA in the territory of the municipality of Urosevac, like on the 3rd of April in the village of Grebno, where 11 ethnic Serbs were attacked? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the same day, in the village of Gatnja in the same municipality, terrorists asked local Albanians to join them and the latter refused?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not here to testify to this. These are things of no interest to me and I have no knowledge of that. This would just waste our time. I don't know why he's asking me these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, indeed, Mr. Bucaliu, and thank you for reminding me to do my job. But Mr. Cepic, the Slobodan Milosevic style of cross-examination will not go down well here, I can tell you. And this -- this method of --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- putting propositions that you have a pretty confident idea the witness is going to know nothing about is not an appropriate way to conduct cross-examination in this particular trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I understood, Your Honour. I just asked for the neighbourhood villages. I do apologise to this Honourable Trial Chamber if I waste some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bucaliu. I haven't got any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning. I assume that I'm going to be the one who's going to have problems with this log-book, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bucaliu. I am Aleksandar Aleksic, attorney-at-law, and together with our lead counsel, Mr. Ackerman, and with my colleague, Mr. Aleksandar Vujic, I am on the defence team of General Nebojsa Pavkovic. On behalf of this Defence team, I am going to put a few sets of questions to you. I'll try to be as accurate as possible when I put these questions, and I am going to ask you to give me the briefest possible answers to my questions, possibly yes or no only. Would that be all right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try. Depending on your questions, I will answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bucaliu. I am going to start my line of questioning with something that my colleague Mr. Cepic started and that has to do with assistance that you gave to a member of the KLA -- or actually, sorry, before that. You gave two statements to the OTP, to the Office of the Prosecutor of this court. And you testified in the Milosevic case on the 12th and 13th of March, 2002. In addition to that, the first statement that you gave to any organisation that we are aware of and that has to do with the events that you are testifying about is a statement made to an international called the International Crisis Group. Is that right? That was in Macedonia in the Stankovac camp, Stankovac I?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement I gave in Stankovac in Skopje, they were sent to the offices of the Tribunal in Skopje. So the only statement I gave was the one I gave to the Tribunal staff in Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You are saying that you did not give any statement to an organisation called the International Crisis Group while you were in the Stankovac camp, right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't give any other statements to any other body.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sorry. I would like to ask that we show 4D12 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. -- we shall do that, Mr. Aleksic, but the witness has acknowledged he did give a statement. The question is where, if you can clarify that. And it may be that he's not aware of the exact identity of the group that took the statement. But let's see it and see if that clarifies anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sorry, I have just been informed now that it's not there. I would kindly ask the usher to put the B/C/S version of the statement on the ELMO for the witness, and for the Trial Chamber we have sufficient copies in English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could the English please be placed on the ELMO because then it can be used by all booths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please put the English version on the ELMO and give the witness the hard copy of the B/C/S, which he I think can read.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I also have an Albanian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's even better. Give the witness, please, the Albanian version. Please carry on, Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In that statement that is in front of you, you refer to -- or rather, there is an incident number 2 that is mentioned and then the second sentence that is -- the sentence that I'm referring to. "On the 4th of April, 1999, two buses arrived, two houses were burned, and that's when the road to the village was blocked."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, we cannot hear the speaker because other microphones are on in the court-room.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then, Mr. Bucaliu, as you were testifying in the case against Slobodan Milosevic in the direct examination by Ms. Romano, on page 2063 of the transcript, in response to her question about the burning of houses you said: "On the 3rd of April, that's when the torching took place -- sorry, it was on the 5th of April." And then on the same page in line 16 you say: "Four houses were burned." And yesterday on page 71 of the transcript, lines 18 and 19, you said that two houses were burned. And just one more thing in relation to this. Finally, in the cross-examination when you were cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic on page 2088, line 1 -- or rather, lines 1 through 4, in response to similar questions put by him your answer was: "Possibly I referred to the wrong date for the first four houses that were burned." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I object. That's a compound question. I'm not sure which he's being asked to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm not sure about that, Mr. Hannis. I'm waiting to hear how the answer goes. Let's hear. Can you answer that question, Mr. Bucaliu, or do you wish it broken down into smaller pieces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the answer was given by the gentleman himself. The date may have been put wrong. I didn't pay much attention to the exact date. What is important for me was the event that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, he's putting to you a question that in your evidence you said that four -- your evidence in Milosevic, you said that there were four houses burned on the 5th of April and that yesterday you said there were two. Now, he's looking for clarification of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying this. Yesterday I said two and at that time I said four. You should know that seven and a half years have passed, and to be frank with you you may not be very exact as to the number. What matters for me is that some houses were burned. It may have been two, three, or four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you to Mr. Bucaliu, too. I understand it's been quite a while, but on page 2088 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note that they cannot hear the speaker because other microphones are on in the court-room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just ask if anyone who's not speaking to put the microphone off, please, because it seems to be disturbing the interpreters. It's probably me of course, but I'll try to keep as quiet as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question, Mr. Bucaliu. I beg your pardon. On page 2088 of the transcript in the Slobodan Milosevic case, line 12, you said: "Possibly I mentioned the wrong date in the case of the first houses." Is that correct? And then I can move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like to continue along the lines of something that Mr. Cepic started dealing with, and that is the assistance that you gave to this KLA soldier. I would kindly ask you to look at -- or actually, I don't know whether you have your second statement, the one that you gave in 2001. If you don't, I have an English copy here and an Albanian copy as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could the usher please assist us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I be clear on the purpose of this line of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in this statement that I have just referred to now, the witness spoke in a different context of the time when he helped this soldier, about when it happened. So that's what I would like to explore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And how is that going to help us in deciding the questions that are before us in the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, yesterday on page 72 and 73 of the transcript in response to different questions, you spoke of how you distinguished between this first group of uniformed men and these others who came on the 5th of April. And then in response to the question put by Mr. Hannis, namely how old the soldiers were who had been in the village before that and who you described as the regular army, and in response to this question you said: On the first day these three soldiers were around 40 years old. Later on I saw some other soldiers, some younger, some older. Now, you were born in 1957, Mr. Bucaliu. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And as you said yesterday, you did your military service in the Yugoslav People's Army in 1976/1977; right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Which is to say that at that time -- which is to say that at that time you were 20 or 21, like most soldiers who do their regular military service?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was 19 when I did my military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Bucaliu. My question is whether you know in your day and later on what the age limit was -- or rather, what the maximum age was for soldiers, when -- at what age were men called up to do their regular military service. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was from 18 to approximately 32. This is what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I'm putting it to you that the age span was 18 to 27. But I will move on to my last topic. Mr. Bucaliu, I mean -- well, it has to do with trains and the train log-book. Mr. Bucaliu, yesterday on page 84 of the transcript, lines 10 and 11 and so on, you said that before the 24th of March there were ten trains within 24 hours; five in one direction, five in another direction. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can look at the log-book. Some day there were ten, some days not. Give me a date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, can you indicate to me the purpose of this line of cross-examination now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm trying to prove that in the period from the 25th of March until the 3rd of April nothing much was happening -- or rather, the trains, as the witness said, were not operating for five days, yes. And after that there was only one train in two days. I mean, absolutely there wasn't any major increase, in terms of trains that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why can't you just make these submissions based on the log-book in due course at the end of the case? I don't think anyone's arguing with you about that. If all you're going to do is get the witness state what is obvious from the log, there's no point. We don't have the luxury of that -- time for that sort of exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In yesterday's transcript page 86, lines 21 through 25, and page 87, lines 1 through 3, you were answering questions put by my learned friend Mr. Hannis and you were talking about train 31781. And he also mentioned 37890, that was an even number, and that those were the two last trains for the 31st of March. And then he asked you about this arrow. He asked you about 37891, what that arrow meant, and you said that that meant that the train did not stop in Urosevac. And now I am asking you to kindly look at the other train, the even-numbered one, that returned from the border, if I understood it correctly, 378 -- just a moment, please. Yes, yes. ERN number K0218505. I see an arrow there, too. Mr. Bucaliu, what does that arrow mean?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please indicate the date you want me to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Mr. Bucaliu. The 31st of March, the last train for the 31st of March. So the page is K0218505.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me what does the arrow mean after the train number. I already said, even yesterday, that the arrows indicate that the train passed through the Ferizaj station but didn't stop there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, in relation to some of these trains, for example, the next one, the first -- the first train on the 1st of April, it's just a line that's there rather than an arrow. Does that mean the same thing or does that mean something different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should have been an arrow. If it is a line, it should be horizontal, otherwise it should have been an arrow. But the person who has noted down that should have put an arrow also there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What would a horizontal line mean then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the same page you have the 29th and you see a horizontal line, which means that the train arrived at Ferizaj but didn't -- stopped there, didn't go on. And on the same occasion 7892 train set off from the Ferizaj station. This train --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... at Ferizaj, yes, I understand that. Thank you. Now, is there anything else on the log-book, Mr. Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question and I'm going to finish my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, carry on with that question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, in this document that you explained to us in detail there is no information about the number of passengers and number of train cars. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes, it's true. There is no number for the carriages and for the passengers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bucaliu.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Aleksic. Mr. Visnjic, do you have any questions -- Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, do you have questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have a few and I'm afraid that it is -- they would be mainly regarding this log-book, but I think that you will accept my reasoning why do I have to ask these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Right. Well, we will take up these questions when we resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bucaliu. My name is Branko Lukic, and together with my learned friend Dragan Ivetic and Mr. Ogrizovic, I appear today on behalf of Sreten Lukic. Yesterday we heard that you worked on keeping the transportation log-books up until 1987 and after that you continued your employment with the railway company. Would you agree with me if I said that it was standard occurrence to see or to have police escort on every train. The same would go for 1986, 1987, as well as for 1996, 1997, and afterwards?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be a normal occurrence, but local trains were not escorted by the police. International trains, yes, but not the local ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that local trains never had any police escort?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say -- I can't say that they never had any police escort, but this police escort was not on regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the presence of the police in a railway station in order to maintain law and order and to try and prevent any criminal acts from happening?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say it is a common thing, but it wasn't again on regular basis. From time to time there was police presence in railway stations, but not always.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. By leave of the Chamber, I wanted to ask you something concerning the transportation log-book. Based on yesterday's transcript when His Honourable Judge Bonomy asked Mr. Hannis: [In English] "What in all these details of the trains have we to pay attention to, just the trains that Mr. Bucaliu was on?" [Interpretation] Mr. Hannis responded: [In English] "No, Your Honour, he's talking about the general train schedule, how many trains went on an average. You can see from the log-book that the number of trains increased. You can read from his testimony about how additional cars were put on it." [Interpretation] Mr. Bucaliu, it is our Defence's position, and you will say otherwise if you disagree, that the number of trains after the 25th of March, 1999, until the 19th of June, 1999, when we have the last entry in this log-book, that the number of trains was drastically reduced. Since I don't think the Bench has the translation of the full document, I wanted to put the following to you and perhaps you can tell us whether you know something about it. During the 88 days, if there were ten trains a day, it would amount to 880 trains in total. I counted the trains entered in this log-book, and in the aforementioned period instead of 880 there were 228 trains. Is it your testimony still that the number of trains increased after the beginning of the NATO campaign?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the number of trains increased after the NATO air-strikes began during the period from the 31st of March and onwards, but then there was another period when the number of trains was reduced. And as for this period, when the number of trains was increased, these were trains that were running outside the normal schedule. These were trains that were designated to transport people from Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, I was trying to save some time rather than going from one day to the next in this log-book. It is my position that out of the 88 days there were only two days during which there were more than ten trains a day. This was on the 2nd of April and the 3rd of April. In the other 86 days out of a total of 88 there were less than ten trains a day. And I'll tell you the following: There were not nine trains on any of the 86 days. There were eight trains on only one day, on the 31st of March, 1999. Seven trains a day, that happened on two days. Six trains a day, four days. Five trains a day, not a single day. Four trains a day, on nine different days. Three trains a day, on five different days. Two trains a day, on 53 days --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have only two more numbers, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but so what. This is a speech you are making --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is absolutely in contradiction what this witness is claiming and this is -- he is brought because of this. This will show you us that the number of trains --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is a speech. Just a moment. Mr. Bucaliu, are you saying that the log-book accurately records all the trains that pass through the station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is recorded very accurately. No train can pass through the station without being marked in the log-book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why do you need to ask these questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To impeach this witness. He is claiming that the number of trains, as we heard right now, increased --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you mean impeach the witness? You've got the document that on the face of it contradicts what he's saying. What more do you need? You just get his answers repeating that he disagrees with what you're putting to him. Is it not sufficient that he accepts that this is an accurate record and then you can point to the point that it doesn't show more trains?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If that satisfies Your Honours, that satisfies me as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What else would you achieve by going through a detailed cross-examination of the numbers? Tell me what you think you are going to achieve by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You wanted to figure out yesterday as well from the Prosecution why this witness is brought in to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was confused as well because he is claiming, based on this document, that there is the increase of the trains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That actually deported people outside the Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, all of this is obvious from the transcript in the Milosevic trial, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't think --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Maybe I don't read that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you read the log -- well, okay, you can. But I really don't see how you're going to advance matters by going through a speech of listing all these figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can I read two more numbers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. You can proceed to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. Give me one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have only a few questions, maybe only a couple. Mr. Bucaliu, having worked with the railway company did you know of the fact that movement in the border area is limited in peacetime so that passengers cannot leave a train or a bus on which they are travelling. They can't even get out of a passenger vehicle. Do you know that movement in the immediate border area is restricted?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Bucaliu. We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you look at page 2127 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Give me one moment. Yes, Your Honour, I'm on that page. Can you help me with the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I'm just -- from then on you'll see that the Court in that trial questioned the witness about the log-book. Are you telling me it's not obvious from that that he was giving evidence on the basis of the material in the log?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is obvious. That's why I'm not clear with the Prosecution's claim that it shows the increase of the number of trains. If they stipulate that there is no increase, there wouldn't be any confusion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Hannis, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, when Mr. Cepic asked you about when your uncle's truck was taken away, did any of the Serb soldiers advise you that you were entitled to be compensated for that?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that they did not invite me to any right of compensation. Simply, the keys were grabbed from my hand. He said that he would just want to check what is in that truck, but he didn't do that. He simply started the engine and left, and this is the truck they used to loot some warehouses, Albanian warehouses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take it then you didn't get any receipt for your truck as well?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no receipt at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The last question I have for you relates to the log-book --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll ignore the reference to the looting of Albanian warehouses, Mr. Hannis. That's material -- that hasn't arisen -- doesn't arise out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to page 20, line 14 from today, Mr. Cepic asked you about the log-book and the fact that your signature doesn't appear in that log-book because during this period of time, as you testified, you were not keeping the book. But there were other signatures in the book; correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. These are the signatures on my colleagues who made the entries in the log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you recognise those from having worked with those individuals and being familiar with their handwriting?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can recognise the signature of each and every one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Now, Mr. Cepic, the map was marked by the witness, and if you wish it to be an exhibit, we would give it an IC number. I understand that a picture of the marked map has been taken and therefore is available for a number now. So shall we give it a number?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. Thank you. For clarification, as regards the map the witness said he drew the map, and I don't know what validity or what probative value it would carry once admitted. [In English] -- clarification on that map, it is just one clarification. It is so difficult if I see four Cs, letters on that map, which is insignia of Serbian -- that is a Serbian insignia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, that may be, but what we have is the evidence that the witness has given. We have the document. You wish it to --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- to be given an exhibit number and that will now be given to it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC32, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Mr. Bucaliu. That completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to give it, and you're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, as well. We couldn't elaborate many things during my testimony, but I hope you have the transcript of my testimony from the Milosevic trial. But my opinion is that many things remained unelaborated during this testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we have a -- we have a full account of all the evidence you gave in the Milosevic trial. So thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, who is your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Carter will lead the next witness, who is Florim Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the basis of this witness's evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: He is 92 bis (B), Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The paragraphs of the indictment that are dealt with in this evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: That would be paragraph 72(j) and 73, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, and additionally 75 and 77 generally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, we already have before us information in written statements which you have given, so we know a lot of the material that you can present to the Tribunal already. The purpose of the hearing today is to enable counsel who appear for the Prosecution and for the accused to ask you questions, either to add to what you've said, to clarify what you've said, or to challenge what you've said. The important thing, because we already have so much material in front of us, is that you listen carefully to each question and answer that specific question and try and confine your answers to the narrow boundaries of the question. If one of the counsel wants more information, then he or she will simply ask you another question. It's as simple as that. So please restrict your answers as far as possible to answer the particular question posed. The first counsel to ask these questions will be for the Prosecution, and that will be Ms. Carter. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The 92 bis package involved with this witness is P number 02269. I additionally have a hard copy of the witness's statement in Albanian that I'd like to have him take before him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I -- I have at the moment, and you can perhaps confirm that this is accurate. I have two witness statements. Is that wrong?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And does he -- is he being given a copy of both of these?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: He's given a copy of the primary statement. The additional statement was simply on the -- to correct one item. I can certainly give him a copy of that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the one you've given him is the 23rd of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, when you came in for proofing, did you have an opportunity to review this statement?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: [No verbal response].

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you answer audibly?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And do you find that the statement is clear and accurate as the statement you had given on April 23rd of 1999?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, it's 100 per cent accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would request at this time that the statement be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, can you please introduce yourself to the Court, spelling your first and last name, please.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Florim Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And can you spell your last name, please.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: K-r-a-s-n-i-q-i.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, you are a Kosovar Albanian who once lived in Kosovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I still live in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And specifically, your testimony involves the municipality of Urosevac. Is that correct?
