utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to direct you to pages 7 and 8 of your statement in the Albanian; in the English, I'm directing to page 6. Sir, I'm going to ask you briefly about the forces of the FRY in Serbia who were involved in the incidents in Urosevac at the time of your testimony. At a paragraph you indicated that when your convoy was stopped it was stopped by both soldiers as well as paramilitary. Can you please explain to the Court what the difference to you is between a soldier and a paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The difference between a regular soldier of the Yugoslav army and a paramilitary, or called in everyday life reservist, is as follows: A regular soldier is of the age span 18 to 30, while the soldiers who were mobilised only for extraordinary times, they are older than 30. So their age span is between 30 and 60.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So when you were indicating that there are paramilitaries involved on page 6 of the English statement, you're indicating those paramilitaries are VJ reservists as opposed to some other type of unit. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Reservists of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicated that there was a difference with regards to their age between the regular soldiers and these reservists. Were there any other differences in regards to their appearance or their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Another difference between regular soldiers and reservists, except for the age span, is their appearance. Another one would be that the regular soldiers of a regular army have a different military style, whereas the older soldiers have another style. They can be not shaved or not with a regular length of hair.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did they wear similar or the same uniforms between the reservists and the regular soldiers?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: For both sides it was a same uniform, the green uniform or called in the Yugoslav army SMB, the olive-green-grey uniform. It was a camouflage uniform, a mixture of green and yellow.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you seem to have some specifics in regards to what type of uniforms the army wore. Did you have any sort of military service yourself or how have you learned the specifics of the VJ uniforms?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I've learned the specifics of the uniforms because I have also been a soldier of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in the past. I used to wear this uniform, and I can say what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At what time did you serve within the VJ army?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, a soldier of the SFRY army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1985/1986, that's when I completed my military service.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Prior to page 6 in the English you make several references to soldiers; however, you don't make any other references to paramilitaries. That would be on page 5 of the English. Had you come across these paramilitaries, also known as reservists, prior to them stopping your convoy at the end of your time?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I've always mentioned the word "soldier." Now, all these men with weapons in a war, regardless of whether they are soldiers or regular army, they're all mobilised under one uniform, under one command. Therefore, it is not important to make a distinction between paramilitary or military. The important thing is that they were mobilised under the Yugoslav flag.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicate that they were all mobilised under the flag. How do you know that there is some type of coordination between these two groups?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: In my opinion there was a coordination between these groups because they were mobilised in one uniform. If they were other groups, they would have worn other types of uniforms or civilian clothes. But they were in a Yugoslav uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At the times that you were able to see reservists and regular VJ soldiers interacting, did they interact all as one group or were they separated in different locations?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: While I was passing through the village of Sojeva, I've seen them in one group, and as to how they manipulated and what kind of other forms of manipulation they used I don't know because I wasn't present there. But as I was passing through the village of Sojeva, I've seen them as one group.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Further down on page 6 in the English you indicate at some point during the convoy you come across police check-points. Is that correct? In the Albanian it will be pages 7 to 8.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At the time that you see the police check-points, was there any interaction between the police and the VJ?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I would like to know to which place you're referring.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicated that shortly after the next soldiers, both reservists as well as regular soldiers, that you headed towards the direction of Urosevac. You continued to see destruction, and at some point when you hit the city limits of Urosevac you came across a police check-point. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, was there any type of interaction between the police and the military?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: During the expulsion from the village as we set off in the direction of Dardani village and took to Ferizaj road, we turned right to Sojeva village. And there we saw a check-point, I've mentioned it in the statement, that there the -- the column was halted for a while. Then we continued in the direction of Ferizaj. At the entrance into Ferizaj there were two policemen. They were traffic policemen. They only made a sign with their hands for us to go back in the direction of Skopje, in the direction of the border with Macedonia. As for soldiers, I have seen them in the village of Sojeva and Bibaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: As you were being deported out of Kosovo while you were on the convoy lines outside of these check-points, were there any military or police escorting you or guiding you along those routes?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: You mean from Ferizaj on 15th of April to Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The convoy of buses heading to Macedonia was not escorted. It was only the buses loaded with people and heading towards Elez Han. It was not under escort.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now I would like to direct you to pages 3 and 4 to the Albanian, and pages 2 and 3 in the English, and I want to discuss with you the occurrences that took place on or about the 4th of April of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that when we provide the references we provide for all three languages because -- or four languages -- that are in use, so I would kindly ask my learned friend to provide us with B/C/S version as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: That would be B/C/S pages 2 and 3 as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Throughout pages 2 and 3, you indicate that there was a mass influx of people into your village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And while these people began to enter your village, you make several references within your statement that there was some sort -- originally there was a registration period that then stopped and then some type of group is providing housing to these individuals who were entering your village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Court what was this organisation that was active within your village who was assisting these internally displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. With the outbreak of the war, first it broke out in Drenica. From there the population began to be displaced. Since they had not left Kosova at that time, we undertook to do this job on a voluntary basis, trying to help the displaced people --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Let me stop you for just a moment. You're indicating that "we are beginning to help them," who is "we"?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: My means of "we" I have in mind, we, the Kosova people.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Within your village was there some sort of humanitarian organisation that was providing assistance as well?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We were a humanitarian group in our village who engaged in assisting these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Was it a formal group such as the CDHRF, the LDK, some other type of organisation who was providing assistance within your village?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We were members of the LDK, but this thing that I mentioned we did on a voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you say that you were a member of the LDK at that time, what type of assistance or what type of activity was taking place with the LDK within your village?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: At that time the LDK engaged mainly in humanitarian issues, and this went on from the 1990s onwards. For example, we worked on education. I'm talking from the 1990s to 1998, the beginning of the 1990s. As I said, we dealt with education, trying to provide minimum assistance to the teachers with the help of the poor population who provided food-stuffs and such elementary aid. This is what I mean by humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When it came to 1999 after the NATO -- or actually shortly before and during the NATO bombing campaign, what type of assistance was the LDK providing within your village?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Look, until the NATO air-strikes we may say that LDK existed. After the air-strikes, LDK ceased performing former function and dealt only with the humanitarian assistance dealing with the crisis. Prior to 1998 LDK was there, and part of it was the emergency group.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The humanitarian assistance that was being provided, you had indicated previously that it began with registering the internally displaced once they arrived in your village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: This began in 1998, when the war broke out, and the flow of refugees coming from one place, from one commune or municipality, to another was not that big. It was easy for us to identify the people who were displaced. So up until the time of the NATO bombing, we could register the individuals or the families that came to our village. But a little -- prior to the NATO air-strikes when the war started to rage, it was impossible for us to keep registering these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Once the formal registration abilities stopped, did you still continue to take in people within your village?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, speaking for myself, I'm not finding any added value in this line of examination, unless there's something in particular you're veering towards.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. I'll try to specifically ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, when you were involved in the registration period, and even when people were coming into your village later on, was it a part of the LDK's responsibility and ultimately part of your responsibility as being a member of the LDK to interview the persons who were arriving in your village to determine what circumstances they were leaving prior to entering your village?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We continued to question them, to interview them, but it was hard for us to understand what was going on from their recounts, because they were so scared that they were unable to be coherent in what they were telling us. It took some days for us to be able to learn something from them, maybe after a week or so. I remember one instance, a mother who had given birth to a child at night and in the morning the Serbs had drove her away from the village. So you can imagine that situation. She gave birth to her baby at about 2.00, 3.00 in the morning, and at 8.00 in the morning she was driven out of her house.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Specifically, as is detailed within your statement, you talk about several killings that take place in villages that were not your own. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: As a member of the LDK at the time who was providing the humanitarian assistance, was it part of your job to learn about what had occurred to these people and try to determine who was involved?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At the point that you began to interview these people, specifically I would like to address what occurred within the -- the gentleman by the name of Hasim Sahiti in Pojatista which is referenced on page 3 of the English, page 3 of the B/C/S, and page 4 -- excuse me -- yes, page 4 of the Albanian. You start beginning to describe what had taken place with Mr. Sahiti. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: During your investigations with what took place with Mr. Sahiti, were you able to interview and speak with a number of people who provided additional details that corroborated what he was telling you?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You began to become aware of the details of the killings themselves as well as who the victims were. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. At that time you indicated that there were five men who died. You'd indicated that there was a gentleman by the name of Shaban Esati, a man by the name of Adem Esati, a man by the name of Haxhi Godeni, as well as Osman Mehmeti. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: For some reason within the statements, Haxhi's name is given quotation marks. Is that his name or some sort of moniker that was given to him for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, there is. Haxhi's name is in inverted commas because his correct name is Bajram. The name Haxhi is used because, according to our religion, we are supposed as Muslims to go to the Mecca, and the person who returns from the Mecca is called Haxhi from that time on. So I didn't know his name and during the funeral ceremony I found out that he was a Haxhi because of the cap he was -- he had on his head. And I said Haxhi was from Godenj village living in Ferizaj. That's why I called him Haxhi Godeni. But afterwards I found out that his true name was -- real name was Bajram.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. You also indicated that you were present at the burials of some of these men. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ob English page 4, B/C/S page 4, and Albanian page 5 you indicate --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. This is really not helping us. We need a paragraph number, and we provide the paragraph number each time. So we have to have the paragraph number, or give us five, six minutes to go through the whole page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you as a trained lawyer are perfectly capable of very quickly scanning a page of typed script, and it doesn't help your cause to exaggerate your predicament. I agree with you that it would be helpful for all of us if all the statements simply had paragraph numbers rather than page numbers, but we have to do our best with what we have, and the one I have certainly doesn't have paragraph numbers and I'm not finding any real difficulty at the moment, but no doubt Ms. Carter will do her best to assist you as far as she can.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In the B/C/S that would be page 4, the second full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you'd indicated that you were present at the -- during the burials of these gentlemen who died. You also indicated within that paragraph that there were four grave-sites, yet you only attended the funerals of three men. Can you please explain the discrepancy between these two?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I can. During -- when the Yugoslav army or the Yugoslav soldier executed these persons, they were -- their bodies remained there on the spot where they were killed. Shaban Dema Esati, the first person, who was about 70, his son Ademi was 45, 50, and Bajram Haxhi Godeni or Haxhi Godeni as I referred to him in my statement; I explained to you I didn't know his name before. The three other persons, the one from Asmir, from Smir, he was wounded. He was lucky enough to escape being killed because the bullet hit him in his wrist-watch -- in his pocket-watch.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the bullet ricocheted and wounded him in his leg. The other person, Osman Mehmeti, was wounded in the belly and on his leg. He tried to drag away from the place he was shot, and he was brought to my neighbourhood and administered the first aid, but because of -- he had lost a lot of blood and because we lacked proper medication, he died at 1.00 the next day. He was buried in the mountain too. He was buried by some other persons. At that time I was dealing with other people, trying to find shelter for them and provide assistance to them, food-stuffs and so on. So these other people buried Osman Mehmeti in the mountain. After 16 or 1700 hours, one day later, after they were executed, the relatives of these persons pulled out the dead bodies from that place and took them to a mountain-path to that meadow that I have drawn on the map. And I attended the burial ceremony of these three persons. We dug some holes, about 50, 60 centimetres deep, and we buried them in their clothes without moving anything. We just threw some mud over their bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi, that will be enough for this incident. We have got to make some progress now. We have many other things to cover.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Last topic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you had also indicated that there were any number of people who were arriving within your village, and you were trying to attempt to locate housing for them. What type of life or housing were these internally displaced people subjected to at the time near the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: During their displacement we tried to find shelter for them, but it was hard for us. We -- sometimes we sheltered 40, 50 persons in a single room. They couldn't lie down or sleep. Other than the housing, we had to provide other necessities to them. We tried to accommodate them anywhere, not only in houses, just for them not to be out in the street. So when I say "housing," just to put them inside a place. They had a roof over their heads.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: With this large influx of people within your village, was there a common theme of what made them leave their homes, albeit NATO bombing, Serbian aggression, or some other reason?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Serb aggression.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. General Lazarevic, General Pavkovic, and thereafter we'll follow the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Krasniqi. I'm Mihajlo Bakrac, Defence counsel for General Lazarevic. First of all, I would like to clarify one particular point with you. I don't find this clear. You said that you were a member of the Democratic League of Kosovo. Is that a humanitarian organisation or a political organisation?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I can explain that to you. I can tell you that after you amended the constitution by force of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia you changed the status of Kosova and you registered all the other parties, your parties, but not the LDK which --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave I really don't have too many questions for this witness and I can move quickly through the cross-examination; however, if I keep getting this kind of answer -- I mean, I did not change the constitution of Kosovo and I was not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the -- go back to the question. Would it not be fairly obvious that it's a political organisation carrying out some humanitarian work? Or is it more complicated than that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's precisely what I asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think that's fairly obvious from what we've been hearing, is it not? Anyway, if you feel the need to explore it further, please do. We all know that the LDK is a political party. I don't think you need to spell that out to us and we've heard it does some humanitarian work.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, since we've clarified this matter, we know it's a political organisation. Now I'm interested in the following. This organisation of yours, did it strive for -- or rather, was one of its main principles striving for an independent Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: With the founding of the LDK, its main objective at the beginning was for Kosova to have the status of a republic in the context of the SFRY; whereas after the outbreak of the war in the entire territory of the former Yugoslavia the term came for Kosova. So the objective changed after that, full independence for Kosova. I believe that this is common knowledge, so your question seems rather ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi. Mr. Krasniqi, I followed your testimony before and I just wanted to suggest that we -- to you that it is not up to you to assess the value or the validity of my questions. Could you please focus on providing answers and answers alone. Thank you. When did you become a member of that political organisation, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, don't answer that for the moment. Don't answer the question, please. Help me to understand the relevance of all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave I was about to discuss the topic. I wanted to know whether he was a long-standing member of the Democratic League of Kosovo, and then my following question would be whether he knew that there were some armed members and KLA members within his organisation. This is my line of questioning. I wanted to know whether he engaged in humanitarian work as of 1990 or as of some later date. But I don't know whether I should get into such questions because now I've revealed my intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why do you think these questions help us? I mean, what is it you're going to say? That he's lying to us? That we can't rely on him? Is that what you're saying? Or is it just -- are you building some case of your own about the KLA? What is the purpose of the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wanted to hear his answers on some questions I deemed important, and if I told you everything I was going to ask this witness then there was no longer need for me to ask the witness those questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but I'm not asking you to do that. I'm asking you to tell me the objective of the cross-examination. What are you seeking to achieve?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to see whether his organisation, for which I believe was numerous in his area, and having in mind the length, duration, of his membership, to know whether it participated in any armed activities. This was my main intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, proceed to ask these questions if that -- you think that that will produce the answers that will help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Honour, I don't believe I will get any helpful answers now. But nevertheless, I will continue with my questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't understand that comment, Mr. Bakrac, because you've done nothing, nothing has happened that will prevent you asking the question. And we have at the moment no reason to doubt that the witness will try to answer them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then, Your Honour. I will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell me when did you become a member of the Democratic League of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: As of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How many members did the Democratic League of Kosovo have in your village?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: During the founding time, and from that time about 17 years have passed, it has -- at the time there were over 100 persons, members.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Before the outbreak of the war, before 1999, before the NATO campaign, how many members did it have?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I told you, this entails a long period of time. I said over 100. I cannot give you an accurate figure. I was not the secretary of the LDK branch --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, you're being asked to estimate how many members there were as at March 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said earlier when the Prosecutor asked me that before the NATO air-strikes until January 1999, the LDK functioned. After 1999, January, we all started to engage with humanitarian affairs, not with party affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, the question is a simple one. As at March 1999 in your village how many members of the LDK were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1999, March 1999, the members of the Presidency of the LDK were 11, but the broad membership, this number can be provided only by the secretary. I cannot give you an accurate figure. I know only that they are over 160, 170 in March 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I wanted to draw your attention to the fact that in the Milosevic case you said that there were 200 members of the LDK. First you said 100 now and then in the supplemental information you said before the outbreak of the war in my village there were ten members of the LDK --

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I just said that ten members form the Presidency of the LDK branch. This is what I said. Please understand me correctly. I just stated that there were over 150, maybe 200. If I say "over 150" I may mean much more than that, but I cannot give you the exact number of the members because I was not the secretary of the LDK branch. I believe that the membership number doesn't matter much --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bakrac where in the supplemental information do you find the figure of ten members?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, paragraph 3, this is the English version as well as the B/C/S: [In English] "LDK staff members in the village."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is the main statement you are talking about on the 23rd of April --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is a note on supplemental information dated the 1st of September, 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, that's something I don't have. That's -- I thought it was something that had been handed to us. All right. Anyway, you have the explanation. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it also true that you said that after the NATO bombings, out of the ten only five members remained. This is also in the supplemental information sheet.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Five members remained in the leadership of the humanitarian group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, you say that after January 1999 you started engaging in humanitarian work and that you abandoned your previous activities. What were these previous activities?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The work we did before was to deal mainly with educational issue. As you might know, we collected a symbolic amount of money to pay the teachers, like 20, 30 Deutschmarks, as a salary. This was a kind of humanitarian issue because everybody knows what the situation of education in Kosova was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I believe you will agree with me that a great number of the Democratic League of Kosovo members were also members of the KLA and that they carried arms. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: From Ferizaj to Gjilan there wasn't any KLA army; this I know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you carry arms?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: None of the 200 members of the Democratic League of Kosovo was armed, those from your village?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Not only the 200 members of the LDK in my village, but not even a single inhabitant in my village was armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I know that because this is where I was born, this is where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, when Mr. Hasima -- no, sorry, Hasim Sahiti told you about that event in the village of Pojatista, he said that soldiers took him and another five men to go from one house to the next and the houses turned out to be empty and that after that they started leaving the village and moving towards the nearby forest. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And on that day, this being the 5th of April, the people of Pojatista arrived in your village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that in the Milosevic trial regarding the recovery of the bodies of these people you said the following. This was page 4483 of the transcript: "We learned about that because the son of Osman Mehmeti and Shaban's son Muharrem went there after Hasim had told them where the firing was. Their lives were in danger because the shooting continued while they were trying to approach the location. They crawled to that place and they recovered the wounded and the killed." If the village of Pojatista was empty, as you were told this by Hasim who said that all the houses were empty and if all the inhabitants of Pojatista had come to your village, what sort of firing did such people have in mind, the firing that went on so that they needed to crawl? I put it to you that there was fighting there between the KLA and the Serb forces. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's not correct, that there was a fighting between the KLA forces and the Serb forces. There was no KLA in that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Krasniqi. Please explain to me then whether the Serb forces opened friendly fire at each other, since this is what you stated in the Milosevic trial. You stated that there was firing there still and that they had to crawl to recover the bodies.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: These people were executed at a location between Mirosale and Pojatishte village, so in the vicinity of a mountain. The family members of those who died, they crawled to the mountain to recover the bodies. But there was nobody there. Now, as to why they were shooting, I don't know. They should know that. Now, whether they were celebrating something or not, I don't know that. If I was not present there -- if I was present there at that moment, I wouldn't have been here today to testify; I would have been dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krasniqi. I understand, and this answer of yours suffices. I will move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, in that case we'll take the break there, Mr. Bakrac, before you move on, and we'll resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I can see you still putting on your headphones. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, before the break we were discussing the incidents described to you by Hasim Sahiti. In your statement given to the OTP on the 23rd of April, 1999, you stated, and I will quote only the latter portion because the initial portion we discussed already concerning the movement from one house to the next. One of the officers was told to take out those people and take them out of the village, and you had in mind the five or six men. And then they went together with a soldier who accompanied them out of the village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: When the Serb forces entered that village, they expelled every family from the village. One part of the expelled people remained in the mountains and another came to our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I apologise if I was imprecise. This is all in your statement. I'm interested in the following. You said that those five or six men -- or rather, that an officer told to -- told a soldier to take those people out of the village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: This is exactly what I wanted to elaborate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, I don't need any more details. Just tell me whether this, what is in your statement, is correct, this information you received from Sahiti.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: This statement of Sahiti is accurate, the way it is written in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Excellent. And after that you said that you were told by Sahiti that once they came close to the forest a burst of gun-fire could be heard and Sahiti started running. Is that correct as well?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, therefore Mr. Sahiti wasn't able to tell you at all who opened fire. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The fire was opened by the Serbian soldier on these six persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How do you know that when you now confirmed what Sahiti told you exactly? Once close to the forest a burst of gun-fire could be heard and I started to run, this being Mr. Sahiti. Everything else is your speculation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: He, Sahiti, Mr. Sahiti, told me exactly what happened. Secondly, they were at the foot of the mountain --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And you stated that precisely that way in your statement of the 23rd of April, 1999. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The way he told me, that is the way I described it. But in addition to his statement I saw the victims that I buried myself. Adem Sahiti [as interpreted], it was horrifying to see his body, what had it become because of the bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Krasniqi, I am happy with your answer and I will move on. The next event that you described is on the 7th of April when you saw from a distance some smokestacks and fires, and it seemed to you that in Kamena Glava and Sojevo villages there were houses on fire. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And on that same day you heard that seven people had been killed in Sojevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And then on the next day, on the 8th of April, you noticed that several military vehicles started from Sojevo towards your village and you saw those vehicles approach your village. Then you saw some soldiers leaving the APCs. Is that correct as well?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And this caused great fear and panic with you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Not only with me but with the entire population.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. And after that you left your village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness has already confirmed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- that the whole statement is accurate. Can we move forward to the question now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will cut it short then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said that you came across a check-point and this was after you left your village out of fear, that there were two soldiers at the check-point, and that two of the villagers ran back as the soldiers were shooting in the air. And then you turned your convoy towards Urosevac and started moving towards the village of Sojevo. Therefore, out of this great fear you started moving towards a village for which you know had been set fire to the previous day and where seven people had been killed. Weren't you afraid to go to the village of Sojevo? For your sake and the sake of your family you said that at the control point -- at the check-point you changed the direction of the convoy because you were afraid for your family and then you went to the village of Sojevo where there had previously been burning and murders, and this was precisely the village from which the soldiers came from, those very soldiers that caused fear.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Exactly. After we left the village, at the end of the road we -- these people who were running, they took to the direction of Gjilan, to the village of Tankosic. Their Lada-make vehicle, red colour, was confiscated by the Serbian soldiers and they were sent back. As they were running back, the soldiers were shooting in the air. We thought that they had killed these persons --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, we know all this. You are now reading your statement, and it was just now that Lord Bonomy said that we all have this before us and that we needn't read it. I'm interested in the following. If you fled from the soldiers in Sojevo and if you knew that there were people killed there and the houses set ablaze, how come you started for Sojevo with your family? This is what I want to know. Please don't read back your statement to me.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. If you think that I'm reading my statement here, I can tell you that I don't need a statement. I can tell you live what had happened. Don't think that I'm reading every word of the statement. I will now communicate to you everything that happened and I don't want you to interrupt me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We don't want -- we don't want you to communicate everything that happened. We already have it in front of us. You've been asked a very specific question, which is: When the source of the trouble the day before was Sojevo, why did you head back towards Sojevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we were not permitted to go through Tankosic village. We had to go to another direction. There was no other direction left except for Ferizaj. This was the last direction that we could take. We knew ourselves that we were walking towards the path of death. We were sure of that, but there was no other way out. That's why we were forced to take that direction, either die or there was no other way out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I can assure you, Mr. Krasniqi, that it's far more valuable to everyone here and far more in your interests to answer the question which adds to the information that we have rather than simply repeat something we already know. It must be obvious to you that that is much more beneficial. So please listen carefully to the questions that are being asked. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, you saw two soldiers at the check-point firing in the air and some people were running back, but no one was preventing you to keep moving along that road, this being much safer than going back to Sojevo because you knew of all the things that had happened there. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: These two soldiers stopped the first convoy, confiscated their vehicles. Therefore, we were forced, since they stopped the first members of this convoy, we were forced to take the other direction, towards Sojevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you have any problems passing through the village of Sojevo? Apart from the insults; we know of those. We've read your statement. Were there any other incidents?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Fortunately, there was no other incident, just as it is stated in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi. I wanted one more thing clarified because there is something in your statement which you haven't repeated today in your testimony. Didn't you say in your statement that the members of the paramilitaries had two bands or ribbons on their left shoulder, a blue one and a red one? Today when you were explaining this to my learned friend you didn't mention that, therefore I would like to know whether this thing you mentioned in your statement is correct.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's correct. Nobody asked me for this before, that's why I didn't mention it. But since you raised it now, I'm telling you it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Krasniqi, we are coming to the end of your statement. You said that once you reached the border on the buses, that you gave your ID together with other IDs from the other people in the bus and that you put yours towards the bottom, and you said that you were hoping that they wouldn't check your documents. Can one see from your ID or passport that you were a member of the Democratic League of Kosovo? Is it stated there?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So it's not there. And then you say, to recapitulate, in your documents there's nothing about you being a member of the Democratic League of Kosovo. But then you said: I was concerned that they might discover that I was an active member of the LDK. Does that mean that you took active part -- an active part in the fighting, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, I never in my life took part in fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Why were you afraid of being revealed as an active member of the Democratic League of Kosovo, since it isn't stated anywhere in your documents?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It is not stated in the document, that's true, but I feared that they might recognise since they were exercising violence on some persons, and some persons were even forced to admit things they did not commit. That's why I was scared because they forced people to admit things that they never actually committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi. My last question: Your documents were not seized from you on the border. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, they were not seized. Fortunately, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I thank you for your patience. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will have but a few questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Krasniqi. My name is Aleksander Aleksic, attorney-at-law, and together with John Ackerman and Aleksandar Vujic, I appear on behalf of General Nebojsa Pavkovic. I will have a few questions only for you and please try to be as precise as possible in your answers. If possible, just say yes or no. I will briefly go back to the event you described in detail in your answers to Mr. Bakrac regarding the event with Mr. Hasim Sahiti. In today's transcript at page 56, line 17, you said, talking about that event, you said: "When the Yugoslav soldiers killed those people ..." And then you move on. Therefore, as you said, you didn't personally see those soldiers and you don't know who actually perpetrated that crime? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Personally I didn't see who actually perpetrated the crime, but I just told you what the person who had been there told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question relating to this issue. You say that Mr. Hasim Sahiti told you that this was a Serbian soldier but he didn't describe what he looked like in detail. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I have described approximately the soldiers, how they appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Shaqiri, on page 3 of the English version, and in B/C/S - I don't know about the Albanian version - it's the one-but-last sentence you said exactly what I read out to you: "Hasim told me that this was a Serb soldier but he did not describe him in detail to me." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: He described it in detail when he said that the soldiers was wearing glasses, his uniform was green, this is the description he gave me. It should be in the statement. I really don't understand this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I don't understand you either. That's not what your statement says. At the beginning of your testimony today, you said - and that is line 46 -- or rather, page 46 -- or page 45, line 25 - that your statement dated the 23rd of April, 1999, is 100 per cent correct. I just read out what you stated then. I haven't got my glasses here now, but there is no other explanation. It says here: "He did not describe exactly what he looked like to me." Is that correct, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I know that I have said that he described me, this soldier, as follows, that he was wearing glasses, that he had a uniform. The same thing was said to me by this person from Smira who escaped the execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I'm going to move on to another topic, but I'm telling you today you said: "My statement is 100 per cent correct" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We would ask for a more specific page reference. We are reviewing pages 46 and 45 at line 25, neither of which are giving us the quote that is being stated by my learned colleague about what this witness has testified to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That he said his statement was accurate?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: But he said -- at page 74, line 24, my learned colleague indicates: "It says here he did not describe exactly what he looked to me" in the context of the materials that are on 46 and 45. It's nowhere to be found in either one of those pages and so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, 46 and 45 is where -- or 45 is where he adopts his statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's all that's being said.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Then I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The statement as accurate. That's the only point that's being drawn from these pages. Yeah, please continue, Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, in your statement, in several places, you refer to the Serb army, Serb forces. Is it correct that until the 8th of April when these people got into your village, those people who started running out of a APC, you did not actually see any persons in uniform in that period -- or rather, up until that time. Right?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Up until that time I had seen these kind of forces in Ferizaj exactly on the 25th of March, 1999, not the same people but same forces, soldiers mobilised, tanks --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, in your statement -- I'm sorry. Perhaps I wasn't very precise. You talk about what happened between the 4th and the 8th of April. So the period is from the 4th until the 8th of April. So in that period - I wasn't accurate enough, I'm sorry - did you see anyone like that, up until that moment that is, when those soldiers jumped out of that vehicle on the outskirts of your village and so on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't understand the question now. I thought you were dealing with the position before the 4th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, no. The witness in his statement describes some things that happened between the 4th and the 8th, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I follow it now. Yeah. So, Mr. Krasniqi, you're being asked whether you had seen similar forces between the 4th and the 8th of April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have seen forces that had come from the Gjilan-Ferizaj main road. We had seen them, observed them, from the vicinity of my village. There were trucks towing cannons. They were driving along the Pristina main road and then turned to Tankosic village. Then they stopped there and they were shelling there, the direction towards the Gadime hill and towards Zlatar village. There were four victims in Zlatar village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, this event of the 8th of April, you said that when the soldiers got close to the outskirts of your village started jumping out of the APC and running towards houses. As you said to my colleague Mr. Bakrac, that frightened you and you decided to leave. Did anybody order you to leave the village, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Before they came to our village, we had heard stories from other villages that had been encircled, how many people were killed --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Krasniqi, I asked you a very specific question. You've already told us what it was that you had heard, that you hadn't seen anything yourself. I'm just asking you whether somebody ordered you to leave, yes or no. You don't have to repeat all the other things that are hearsay and that you already described.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: When the Serb soldiers were running in the direction of the houses, in the direction of the yards, it clearly shows that it is cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether somebody had issued you an order, yes or no. Just that. Please don't -- don't start speaking in compound sentences.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Before my neighbourhood there's another neighbourhood, Cakaj neighbourhood, that's where the Serb forces entered. Maybe they issued the order for that particular neighbourhood to leave. And the people from that neighbourhood came to my neighbourhood and we left together. I wasn't present there to see or to speak with the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Pavkovic -- sorry, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. Yeah, sorry, Mr. Petrovic, momentary senior moment. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't want to disappoint you. I have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Krasniqi. I am Branko Lukic, and together with Mr. Ivetic and Mr. Ogrizovic I appear for Mr. Lukic. I hope you have your statement in front of you, so could you please open it. In the Albanian version, page 8, paragraph 3; English, page 6, paragraph 3; B/C/S, page 6, paragraph 2. You're talking about how you came to the town of Urosevac and that you came across a police check-point. You describe the policemen, and you say they told you to turn to Skoplje. Can you tell us approximately how long this convoy was, the convoy that you were moving in?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The convoy that was moving was -- consisted of 30 to 40 tractors, cars. However, when we were directed by the policemen to go towards Skopje, the column split into two. One part went in the direction of Pristina and the other in the direction of Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were you in that convoy; can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I was in the column that went from Ferizaj to Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I meant when you were approaching the check-point. How far away where you from the beginning of the convoy?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I was maybe the 15th or 17th in line, I mean the 15th or 17th tractor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you were not in contact with these policemen. You were just moving behind someone who was moving in front of you?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Nobody contacted that policeman. As I said earlier, he was a traffic policeman. He only gave the sign with his hand. Before we got there, there is a turn there for Ferizaj-Skopje. He just showed a sign with his hand, telling us to go to the direction towards the border with Macedonia. And this shows the ethnic cleansing and the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you set out towards Skoplje, Urosevac is behind you then, right?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Behind, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In order to go back to Urosevac, as you did, you have to turn around at an angle of 180 degrees and take the same road back, right?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: In order to go back to Ferizaj, we used second- and third-hand roads, like field paths. We went through Nekodim village and from there we arrived in Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How much time did you need after you turned around to get to Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: From the Skopje road to Ferizaj or what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please let's deal with this. How far did you get towards Skoplje from that intersection?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: From that intersection we went up to the Sarasel [phoen] village. We took a right turn in the direction of Nekodim village and then we went to Ferizaj through those tertiary roads I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how much time did you need for all that?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this convoy, consisting of a considerable number of tractors and cars, travelled four hours towards Urosevac and no one stopped them. The direction is opposite to the border, right?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. I showed you even earlier, but this delay was due to the fact that the road ran through a flat land. It was a muddy road. Tractors were stuck in that mud, and we were -- we had a lot of -- we ran through a lot of vicissitudes. That's why it took us so long to arrive in Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi. We have no further questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No further questions from the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krasniqi, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming again to the Tribunal to give it. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, our next witness is Bedri Hyseni. In light of the hour, I would ask that we consider an early postponement. And I did want to put on the record and advise Defence counsel of a scheduling matter. We previously had five more witnesses scheduled for this week, and our current intention is to proceed with Mr. Hyseni as the next witness, Mr. Loku, Hazbi Loku, followed by Sejdi Lami, will be the next three witnesses. The witnesses scheduled after that were Isa Raka and Fadil Vishi. Because we were running so far behind and because of their time restrictions on their visas, et cetera, we have arranged for those two gentlemen to return to Kosovo and will bring them back later in the case. Because we need to proceed with the protected witness K73, hopefully starting on Wednesday next week to finish him by Friday, so that a week from Monday we can proceed with the videolink with another protected witness, K82. And that's how we propose to proceed in the upcoming week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you don't want to take 15 minutes to get started, get the documents in and then be ready for -- you're going to have the witness here over the weekend anyway?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. I think I'll go faster on Monday than I will now. He is here and he is available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I dare say if I took a vote I'd be heavily defeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I could probably get six of those guys to give up two minutes of their time along with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I am concerned about progress -- we all are concerned about progress and we're giving it a lot of thought at the moment. We are also concerned that we don't see any obvious signs of a genuine attempt in preparing cross-examination to dispense with the marginally important and concentrate on the really important. That's not to say that the cross-examination in general is entirely or largely inappropriate. We're not saying that. And indeed, in a domestic situation with a much shorter case one could readily understand it. But in this instance it's -- it's going to be necessary to restrict both the extent of the examination where we have the statements and the extent of the cross-examination to a point where we really focus on what is most important. We should also, I think, make it clear that while the use of apparent contradictions in statements or between statements and oral evidence is an obvious -- the identification of these is an obvious route for the cross-examiner to go, in some instances starting at the beginning, working your way through it, and finishing at the end is not really assisting us greatly as professional Judges to arrive at an overall assessment of the witness. So a sense of proportion would be welcomed in the approach to cross-examination that challenges the reliability of the evidence that's being given when compared with what has been said in the past. So we're due to sit again on Monday at 9.00, so we'll now adjourn until then, when we will hear the evidence of Mr. Hyseni.
